case_study_insert.main_stem: Grandview River Tours (GRT) is a private limited company in the tourism and leisure sector, running scenic river cruises and employing a workforce of 24. Founded in 2015 by Ellis Mbeki, GRT uses a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership, letting experienced skippers plan their own routes and commentary. GRT plans to invest $560,000 in two new electric river cruisers, financed by a $360,000 ten-year bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $132,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $62, and currently produces 16,000 units a year, each a booked passenger-trip. GRT faces two problems: sickness absence has reached 8% and customer complaints about crowded cruises are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q2 2025: GRT ran 4,000 passenger-trips last quarter at an average load factor of 71%, down from 79% a year earlier. Complaints about overcrowding rose to 34 per month from 19. Customer satisfaction fell from 4.6 to 4.2 out of 5. Average boarding delay is 11 minutes. A survey of 400 tourists found that 61% would pay $5 more for a small-group eco-cruise, and 49% book their tours through social media. Training records show 9 of 24 crew have not completed on-the-job training in customer care; off-the-job training workshops cost $310 per crew member.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Grandview River Tours as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Travel Bulletin (September 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing costs on GRT's variable-rate bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will increase by 6.2% from $12.80 to $13.59 per hour, raising crew wage costs. (3) Marine diesel prices have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while inbound tourism arrivals grew 5.4% and average household spending on leisure trips rose 2.8%.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for GRT of funding the two new cruisers with a $360,000 bank loan rather than using only retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $360,000 bank loan lets GRT buy both electric cruisers now and begin earning from 16,000 passenger-trips a year, rather than waiting to build that sum from retained profit. Bringing the boats forward raises revenue sooner to cover fixed costs of $132,000 a year and spreads repayment over ten years, matching the years the cruisers will operate. Keeping the $200,000 retained profit available gives a reserve for the rising trade receivables and lower cash shown in Appendix 2.

Point 2: Borrowing leaves ownership and control with founder Ellis Mbeki; no outside investor gains a claim on GRT or a share of future profit. With a contribution of $44 a passenger-trip and break-even of 3,000 trips, GRT has a margin of safety of 13,000 trips, so the loan is well covered. Retaining $200,000 also cushions the 8% sickness absence and the customer-care training bill of $310 per crew member, so expansion does not starve the existing cruises of working capital.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a bank loan over retained profit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to GRT's $560,000 cruisers, trip economics and staffing.

questions.question_text: GRT is promoting its new electric cruisers. Consider national newspaper advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should GRT choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National newspaper advertising: A national newspaper campaign could explain the electric-cruiser story in detail and reach educated readers across the country. The cost is high for a 24-employee operator with a $360,000 loan, and newspapers have a short life and weak visual impact for a scenic product. Much of the readership will be too far from GRT's river to book, so a large share of the spend would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheap, frequent and can reach riverside communities with last-minute trip offers, which suits an average load factor of 71%. Its drawback is a narrow audience: the 61% of 400 surveyed tourists who would pay $5 more for a small-group eco-cruise are not limited to one radio catchment, and GRT needs to fill 16,000 passenger-trips a year, far beyond local demand.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel influencers can show the boats and commentary to exactly the 49% of surveyed tourists who book tours through social media, with videos that demonstrate the small-group experience. Engagement is measurable and targeting is national. Results take time to build and depend on choosing credible influencers, but cost per booking is low.

Recommendation: GRT should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the survey-identified booking channel, supports the $5 eco-cruise premium and scales nationally at low cost. Newspapers are rejected as expensive, untargeted and short-lived, while local radio is rejected as too narrow to lift load factor from 71% to the level needed to justify the $560,000 investment. Influencer footage can also be reused on GRT's own website at no extra cost.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with minimal reference to GRT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two options with some application to GRT's launch and capacity.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why newspapers and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: GRT's sickness absence has reached 8% and complaints about crowded cruises are rising. Explain two benefits for GRT of using laissez-faire leadership with its experienced skippers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership lets GRT's experienced skippers decide how to pace a cruise and adjust commentary when a boat is busy, so decisions are made on the spot without waiting for head office. In a flat structure of 24 staff this speeds up service recovery and can reduce the 34 overcrowding complaints a month, helping protect the 4.2 satisfaction rating and the $62 ticket price.

Point 2: Giving skilled crew autonomy recognises their expertise and raises motivation and job satisfaction, which can ease the 8% sickness absence without costly financial incentives. Skippers who design their own routes are more committed to GRT and less likely to leave, protecting the 4,000 passenger-trips handled last quarter and the $44 contribution on each trip needed to service the $360,000 loan. Autonomy also reduces the need for close supervision in a flat structure of 24, freeing Ellis Mbeki to focus on the electric-cruiser investment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of laissez-faire leadership identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to GRT's absence, complaints and trip economics.

questions.question_text: GRT must train 9 crew members in customer-care procedures for the new cruisers. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at an external workshop. Which should GRT choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Learning on board with senior crew is directly relevant to GRT's own boats, costs no fees and keeps all 9 crew available for the 4,000 passenger-trips run last quarter. It attacks the 34 crowding complaints immediately because staff practise real passenger handling. Drawbacks are that trainers are also working, so tours may slow, and poor habits can spread unless supervisors check standards; formal certification is also weak if tourists demand proof of service quality.

Off-the-job training: The external workshop costs $310 per crew member, so all 9 cost $2,790 — small beside the $560,000 investment — and provides structured customer-care skills and a certificate. It takes crew away from the boats while load factor is only 71%, reducing capacity, and generic content may not reflect GRT's small-group cruises, so on-board follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: GRT should choose on-the-job training with short workshop top-ups later. It is cheaper, boat-specific and avoids losing 9 of 24 staff at a time when 8% absence and 34 complaints already strain operations; full off-the-job training is rejected because the capacity loss and $2,790 cost are harder to justify than practical coaching on the cruisers. Supervisors should sample commentary on every boat each week so consistent standards are kept while crews keep their autonomy; if the 34 complaints do not fall, a short external workshop can be added for all 9 crew. This suits GRT's flat structure, where skippers are trusted to make on-board decisions and the 4,000 quarterly trips stay protected.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to GRT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of GRT's service problem.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to GRT's cruises.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GRT's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $132,000 ÷ ($62 − $18) = $132,000 ÷ $44 = 3,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 3,000 passenger-trips a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $62 − $18 = $44. Answer: contribution per unit is $44.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GRT's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare 3,000-unit break-even with actual output of 16,000 passenger-trips: the margin of safety is 13,000 trips, showing the two new cruisers can run well above break-even and guiding how quickly to add departures.
2. Use the $44 contribution to test pricing: the $5 small-group eco-cruise premium would lift contribution to $49, which can be checked against the 61% of surveyed tourists willing to pay it.
3. Assess loan capacity: with only 3,000 trips needed to break even, the $360,000 repayment is coverable, so managers can set monthly trip targets to protect that cushion.
4. Benchmark unit cost: $132,000 ÷ 16,000 units + $18 = $26.25 a trip, a figure to track each quarter to detect the effect of the 11.3% diesel rise before it eats the $44 contribution.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 3,000 passenger-trips | (ii) Contribution per unit = $44 | (iii) Four uses: 13,000-trip margin of safety, $5 eco-premium modelling, $360,000 loan feasibility and $26.25 unit-cost benchmarking.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GRT's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GRT's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.29 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.24 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.06 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.01 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $18,000 inventories + $55,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $103,000. 2025 current assets = $22,000 + $84,000 + $12,000 = $118,000. 2024: $103,000 ÷ $80,000 = 1.29; 2025: $118,000 ÷ $95,000 = 1.24. Excluding inventories: 2024 ($103,000 − $18,000) ÷ $80,000 = $85,000 ÷ $80,000 = 1.06; 2025 ($118,000 − $22,000) ÷ $95,000 = $96,000 ÷ $95,000 = 1.01.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened slightly. The first measure fell from 1.29 to 1.24 as current liabilities grew from $80,000 to $95,000 faster than current assets, and the second measure fell from 1.06 to 1.01, leaving almost no buffer once inventories are excluded. Cash dropped from $30,000 to $12,000 while trade receivables jumped from $55,000 to $84,000, so at a time when GRT is committing $560,000 to electric cruisers, more of its short-term wealth is tied up in customers who may pay late. That is risky with a $360,000 loan to service.

Conclusion: GRT's financial position has not improved; it has marginally deteriorated. Both measures are lower and the cash fall is the main cause, so GRT should tighten credit control on the higher receivables before drawing further on cash for the cruisers. The $200,000 retained profit going into the boats should be rebuilt first, because cash of only $12,000 covers little of the $360,000 loan commitment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of cash, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on deterioration.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GRT of promoting small-group eco-cruises on the new electric boats.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 400 tourists found that 61% would pay $5 more for a small-group eco-cruise, so the positioning supports a premium on the $62 price and lifts contribution above $44 a trip. It also fits the 49% who book through social media and helps distinguish GRT from crowded competitors, potentially raising the 71% load factor and the 4.2 satisfaction rating.

Disadvantage: Smaller groups mean fewer passengers per sailing, so unless the $5 premium is accepted widely the $44 contribution per trip could fall in total. Electric boats also need charging infrastructure, adding to the $132,000 fixed costs, and if diesel prices are rising 11.3% the environmental benefit may be offset by higher capital and energy spending that the $560,000 budget must cover. Small groups do justify the $5 premium because guests receive more personal commentary, which can raise the 4.2 satisfaction score and support repeat bookings on the two new cruisers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using GRT's survey, capacity and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in marine diesel costs will affect GRT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): If GRT's $360,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 0.75% of $360,000 = $2,700 a year (0.0075 × $360,000). This is small relative to fixed costs of $132,000 a year and would be zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher rates might dampen discretionary tourism spending, but GRT can largely neutralise the direct cost by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.59 per hour): With a workforce of 24, the rise lifts the wage bill for skippers and reception staff and is unavoidable. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an honest annual total cannot be invented; the defensible comparator is productivity of 16,000 passenger-trips ÷ 24 staff = 666.67 trips per worker. If that holds, the higher wage is spread over more trips; if 8% absence persists, unit labour cost rises and the $44 contribution is squeezed.

Diesel cost inflation (11.3%): The $18 variable cost per trip is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is justified: if the whole $18 rose 11.3%, that is 0.113 × $18 = $2.03 a trip, and across 16,000 trips about $32,480 a year. Since the new boats are electric, diesel effects fall mainly on the older cruisers, but the $5 eco-premium cannot fully offset a rise of this size if it feeds into general energy prices.

Conclusion: The 11.3% diesel rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds across all 16,000 trips and directly threatens the $44 contribution that covers fixed costs and the $360,000 loan. The interest rise is a bounded $2,700 and the wage rise can be absorbed if 666.67 trips per worker is maintained.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to GRT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on GRT's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in GRT's context with a justified greatest-impact judgment and reasons why the others are smaller.
